Visual artist Jason Cook  creates kinetic sculptures and robotic installations using electronics, programming and mechanical engineering. In The Walking Chair (2025), an ordinary wooden chair is transformed into a moving machine. A system of motors, mechanical parts and electronic components is attached beneath the seat, allowing the chair’s legs to move. By giving a familiar piece of furniture the ability to walk, Cook changes the way we perceive an everyday object. The chair is no longer simply something we sit on  it becomes an object with a movement of its own. #art #artist #weird #chair #avantgarde

videos.caption: 🚧 Worlds Collide🦈 Phase one is complete, I’m grateful to all for your kind words over the long haul with this one. We all have busy lives, and it’s been challenging to make time for this build. While we’ve got a working finish on the set, I’m planning on adding some additional shine and probably bourlettes (chevron bands above the gums on the teeth). The hinge system allows for articulation in a few ways, I’m pleased with the action along with how the teeth are staggered when closed.  I named this fantasy shark jaws piece ‘Worlds Collide🦈’ because the next phase has nothing to do with sharks or sea life directly. As we slowly roll out phase two, I’m hopeful the work itself will be well received; the addition has to do with flight. Hence, the worlds of sea and air come together. When the grinding dust settles, probably a month or more from now, the overall piece will either be a ‘hero’ or a ‘zero.’😅 I thought this quick trend vid would capture the origin of what used to be  mainly spoons (and horseshoes) — hope you like it. 🙂 Much appreciation goes to @Baileigh Industrial for their support over the years — as long as I’ve had the MPS-2 shear —  circa 2017. The only modification I’ve done to the tool is install a longer arm to allow for the use of less force when cutting.  Thanks again, all, for your continued support. 🙏👊 #baileigharmy #metalart #welding #shark #sculpture

I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

For the past couple of years, @tomasbarcelocastela has been creating robots that combine delicate embossed metal textures with the appearance of old, weathered wood. Wood so aged and cracked that the robots seem to have repaired themselves with staples, rivets, and whatever they could find. When Tomás first started making them, he wasn't entirely sure why. But over time, these details found their place in his personal mythology of Kal's robots. Anat Vel is part of this universe. An anthropomorphic figure inspired by biomechanics, with organic shapes, intricate reliefs, and circular elements suggesting an artificial anatomy. Originally sculpted in fine grog refractory clay, reproduced in resin, and finished with layers of shellac, chalk paint, acrylics, ferric paint, and varnish. And there's something else behind these worn surfaces and carefully repaired bodies: a certain envy these robots feel towards humans.
